Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
John, a 33-year-old married prosecutor from North America, has been grappling with the aftermath of a terrorist attack that occurred six months ago. On that fateful day, he was in court, prosecuting a high-profile case when an explosion rocked the courthouse. The sudden and violent nature of the blast shattered windows and sent debris flying through the air. John remembers the shock and terror as he tried to shield his colleagues and himself from falling debris while chaos erupted around him. The event itself has left an indelible mark on John's psyche, manifesting in a series of triggers that continue to disrupt his daily life. The first is a pervasive sense of exhaustion; John often finds himself feeling very tired or exhausted, even after getting adequate rest. This fatigue is not just physical but also mental, as the traumatic memory continues to haunt him. Another potent trigger for John is the smell of alcohol. He recalls that the terrorists were drunk and their acrid scent lingered throughout the courthouse during the attack. Now, any whiff of alcohol sends a wave of anxiety through his body, triggering flashbacks and intense distress. At work, this has led to avoidance behaviors; he no longer joins colleagues for after-work drinks, which has strained relationships with those he once considered close friends. The sound of explosions or bangs also triggers John's traumatic memories. Even the distant sound of fireworks can send him into a panic. This sensitivity has made his job more challenging as the courthouse often echoes with sudden loud noises from construction and renovations nearby. During these moments, John’s heart races and he feels as though he is reliving the attack, unable to distinguish between past and present. John's memories of that day feel more real and vivid than any other memory in his life. He cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to himself; the sequence of events jumbles in his mind, making it difficult to recount the details without feeling overwhelmed by their intensity. The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over. This inability to process and integrate the traumatic event has left him feeling disconnected from reality. The trauma has also led John to hold onto a series of negative appraisals that further complicate his daily life. He harbors deep feelings of guilt, believing he could have done more to stop what happened or protect others. The memory of not being able to shield colleagues and loved ones from harm is particularly burdensome. This inaction has led John to doubt himself, wondering if he will ever be able to forgive himself for his perceived failure. John also harbors a pervasive sense of distrust towards others. He now believes that people are not what they seem, making it difficult for him to form new relationships or deepen existing ones. This distrust is rooted in the unpredictability and violence he witnessed, leaving him feeling constantly on guard. The cumulative effect of these symptoms has taken a significant toll on John's life. His marriage has suffered due to his emotional distance and frequent episodes of anxiety. He has become increasingly isolated, both professionally and personally, as he avoids situations that might trigger memories of the attack. What finally brought John to seek help was a recent episode where he experienced a panic attack during an important court appearance, unable to continue with his case. This incident was a stark reminder of how deeply the trauma had impacted his life. While seeking help, what frightens him most is the fear that he will never be able to move past this event and fully trust again. Yet, deep down, John hopes for a chance to regain some semblance of normalcy and reconnect with those around him. Through therapy, John aims to confront these fears and learn coping mechanisms to manage his triggers and negative appraisals, hoping to rebuild the life he once knew.
